extracted.intended_audience: readers and creative writers interested in story structure, narrative theory, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Use Christopher Booker’s Seven Basic Plots and related Jungian/archetypal concepts as lenses to analyze or craft stories, assessing plot type, character archetypes, psychological arcs (ego vs Self), and whether elements (sex/violence, sentimentality, moral clarity, community) serve the story. Emphasis on identifying archetypal functions and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven Basic Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Overcoming the Monster, Rags to Riches, The Quest, Voyage and Return, Comedy, Tragedy, and Rebirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one of these plot-types as an organising frame: Booker details the necessary and common elements of each plot and discusses many examples in each chapter. When analysing or constructing a story, identify which of the seven it most closely follows and check for the pattern's key beats and expectations (e.g., quest milestones, voyage-otherworld-return). Be aware of oversimplification and that many stories blend or subvert these types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character archetypes / types
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize recurring character types: helpers (wise old man/woman), the female inspiration/'anima', dark masculine (overbearing father/villain), dark feminine (temptress/witch), senex (dried-up judgmental old man), orphan protagonist, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map story characters to archetypal roles to understand their narrative function and psychological symbolism. Booker provides charts and many examples; the presence, inversion, or omission of these types affects the story's resonance. Watch for caricature (anti-pattern) and for how archetypes manifest differently across cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jungian psychology: ego vs Self
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories often dramatise a battle between the ego (selfish, shadow aspects) and the Self (integrated maturity combining masculine and feminine traits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a story's central arc represents internal psychological movement toward the Self (growth, integration) or toward ego (destruction, tragedy). A happy ending indicates successful integration; tragedy indicates identification with dark power. Use this as a criterion for thematic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster taxonomy and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsters appear in three varieties (often in sequence): Predators ('after something'), Holdfasts ('hold onto something'), and Avengers ('get their own back').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the monster-type(s) to clarify what vice the story externalises. This taxonomy explains the monster's motives and how it embodies selfish/antisocial human behaviour. Beware of forcing examples into the taxonomy when cultural/contextual differences apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage and Return: other-world exposes protagonist's flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: The voyage takes the hero out of familiar frameworks, exposing unconscious assumptions and inner darkness; victory often is internal (overcoming inner darkness), not merely defeating external forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In stories with this plot, assess how the unfamiliar setting reveals protagonist blindspots and whether the return shows measurable inner change. Examples: High Noon, Hadestown/Orpheus (failure can be instructive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy structure and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic comedy includes misunderstandings to be dispelled, lovers reunited, darkness banished/punished; Aristophanic comedy frames an agon between life/liberation and a dark, rigid obsession; the happy ending stems from Recognition (change from ignorance to knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for the comic beats: confusions resolved, transformation through recognition, and the role reversal between above/below-the-line characters. Note that feminine characters often perceive truth and enable male characters to grow. Anti-pattern: using comedy merely to punish outsiders or to endorse regressive social views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy arc stages
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy typically progresses: anticipation phase → dream phase (apparent success) → frustration stage (success slips) → nightmare stage (catastrophe accumulates) → destruction (often self-inflicted death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating tragic arcs, trace these stages and identify the protagonist's fatal flaw and the way bonds to community are broken. The 'call' in tragedy functions as temptation rather than heroic summons. Use this to assess inevitability and moral complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Above-the-line vs Below-the-line dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Above the line' = respectable, conventional society; 'Below the line' = marginalized, chaotic, out-of-sight life; this division often structures comedy and social commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this lens to analyse social strata, comic subplots, and moral perspective in stories. Consider how the line is drawn and whether the narrative privileges or critiques the 'above the line.' Anti-pattern: unexamined elitism that dismisses 'below the line' as simply inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing Whole / Integration of masculine and feminine
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete person (and thus many story resolutions) requires reconciling 'masculine' and 'feminine' virtues; protagonists must integrate both to become whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess character arcs for genuine internal transformation (not just a wedding). Look for internal reconciliation manifesting outwardly in community cooperation and mutual sympathy. Beware of crude gender essentialism—Booker frames these as cultural constructs, but application should be flexible and inclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four signs of imbalance (incomplete/unhappy state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker identifies imbalance as characterised by: (1) aggressive and oppressive use of power; (2) disorder and things not being as they should; (3) things being obscured or hidden so nobody can see whole; (4) a lack of proper feeling, love, or mutual affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four markers to evaluate a story's depiction of disorder and the stakes for restoration. They help diagnose what the narrative must resolve for a 'happy' reintegration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happy ending / liberation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful/happy ending culminates in liberation from the dark power, the prize of integration (community restored), power used wisely and justly, accurate seeing, and friendship/love/reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge endings by whether they achieve internal transformation and communal restoration rather than merely external victory. Look for lasting change (not cosmetic fixes) and evidence of balanced power use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality vs genuine emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality = the false version of something real; it manipulates emotions without corresponding personal reality; it gives a quick thrill but lacks lasting substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether emotional moments arise organically from character and situation or whether they are cheap manipulative cues. Anti-pattern: using sappy climaxes or contrived cues to elicit tears without emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sex and violence (serve story, not titillation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex and violence are plentiful in older stories and can provide transgressive thrill; when used for mere effect they act like a drug needing ever-stronger doses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that sex/violence be motivated by character/plot and contribute to theme or psychological truth. Avoid gratuitous depictions intended only to shock or titillate; impersonal fantasy tends not to mesh with fully realised human characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin myths / Fall as explanatory devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin stories and The Fall explain who we are and often encode psychological/social truths (e.g., 'knowledge of good and evil' as emergence of moral consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or evaluating origin myths, look for metaphoric insights about consciousness, responsibility, and the human condition rather than literal historicism. Use mythic language to probe moral/psychological themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery plot quality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery plots are sometimes 'fluff' (pulp/junk food), but can be substantial when they do more than set up puzzles to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between lightweight puzzle-driven mysteries and ones that use investigation to explore character, society, or theme. Prefer mysteries that integrate psychological stakes and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orphan/coming-of-age motif
rubrics_metrics.description: A striking feature of many myths/folk tales: the central figure is an orphan; the plot often concerns the child becoming an adult against opposing parental figures (senex/dark father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this motif to evaluate rites-of-passage narratives and family dramas. Check how parental/authority figures function as obstacles or catalysts and whether the protagonist's growth is credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wise old person archetype qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wise Old Man/Woman represents complete maturity: travelled the road of inner development, embodies masculine and feminine balance, protective feeling, intuitive understanding, authoritative but not merely old-age stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mentor figures for depth and symbolic function; avoid stock, patronising depictions. Evaluate whether their guidance fosters protagonist integration rather than simply granting answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal voyage / character self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A core marker of 'good' transformative narrative is characters who look inward, gain self-knowledge, and thereby change; absence of this internal voyage yields static, tragic, or resonant-but-unresolved works (Chekhov example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge character arcs on whether they meaningfully engage inner life and change. Recognize that some great works deliberately withhold transformation; that is an aesthetic choice, not necessarily an inferiority, but it should be deliberate and thematically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity and cosmic justice (Booker's evaluative preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker prefers narratives with moral clarity—where good is rewarded and evil punished—and often judges modern works negatively when they lack this cosmic justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when applying this preference: it's a normative criterion (Booker's), not a universal truth. Evaluate whether moral ambiguity serves the work's aims rather than treating lack of cosmic justice as a defect by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egotist / narcissist social function in stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Egotists/narcissists are blind to others (see them as 'below the line'), impose costs on others' time/energy, and spread misery; they map well to comedic and tragic antagonists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify characters whose self-image isolates them from community; assess narrative consequences and how other characters respond. Use this to read social/political allegories (e.g., leaders who harm community).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories as critiques of systems/collective fantasies
rubrics_metrics.description: Authoritarian systems in stories (Nazism, Communism) share features: a collective fantasy/dream, inflated dream-heroes, and designated enemies—lack of genuine balance leads to heartless regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories address political/social systems, look for how they depict collective psychology (fantasy, hero-worship, hate-figures) and whether they show internal contradictions and seeds of destruction. Use this to evaluate sociopolitical relevance and psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural scope and inclusivity (anti-bias criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A caution against overgeneralising from a narrow Western/white-male canon; the book concentrates on Western canon and omits many cultures and works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require analysts and writers to test archetypal claims across diverse cultures and modern works. Omission of relevant texts (e.g., Canterbury Tales) or exclusive focus on Western examples is an anti-pattern that can skew conclusions.
